Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association (MMA)
In Opposition to
LD 358, An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers ofDeeds
February 24, 2025
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on State
and Local Government, my name is Amanda Campbell, and I am submitting testimony on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's 70-member Legislative Policy Committee (LPC) in opposition to LD 358.
This session, the LPC proactively established a platform of bills intended to bolster and support the property
taxpayers of Maine. Through initiatives across the legislative board, they are committed to protecting the interests of their residents and to reducing the burden of property taxes.
LD 558 seeks to increase then fees for certain services provided by a county registrar of deeds. This proposed shift in
cost burden is in direct conflict with the LPC's position.
Municipal tax collectors and treasurers currently pay $19 to record a tax lien and the filing fee is added to the total amount of property tax due by that taxpayer. Additional pages, at a rate of $2 per page, are seldom necessary for lien paperwork. The proposed flat rate of $45 per recording is an increase in upfront costs to the municipality of 158%. This increase results in an additional tax burden for an already delinquent taxpayer and a shift in burden to
the other taxpayers in the community who are paying for those up front filing costs. In addition, this increase could
potentially cause cash flow problems for municipalities that are already juggling tight resources.
For communities that are accessing digital deed records for property tax purposes, the online county platforms are
essential. Any increase in fees to access legal documents necessary for completing the tasks of property assessment directly impact the taxpayers and the LPC requests that municipalities be exempt from those increases.
Municipal officials agree that the costs of doing business are increasing, at both the municipal and county level.
However, instituting statutory service fee increases as an answer to increased costs, without input from those who
require those services to complete statutorily directed assessing work, is not the answer.
Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you and share the municipal perspective on this important topic. Please
feel free to contact me or any member of the MMA Advocacy team with any questions related to municipal
operations.

4 Gabriel Drive, Suite 2 Augusta, ME 04330, 207-623-4697 www.mainecounties.org
LD 358, An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds
February 24, 2025
Chair Baldacci, Chair Salisbury, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government, on behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association, we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony to the Committee in support of LD 358.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all of Maine's 16 counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 358 do? LD 358 would increase the fees paid to a county register of deeds for receiving, recording, and indexing any instrument to $45 per instrument. The bill also increases the fee charged for making paper copies of plans to $10 per page and increases the surcharge a register of deeds may collect to $5 per document. Additionally, LD 358 changes the threshold under which no fee is charged for acquiring electronic images, printed images, or electronic abstracts to 100 images or abstracts in a calendar year. After 100 images or abstracts, a person is charged fifty cents per image or abstract. The bill also prohibits the sale of images or abstracts by persons who download 1000 or more images or abstracts.
Discussion. Registers of Deeds provide critical services to Maine communities, and it is important that the fee structure for these critical services align with the manner in which these services are utilized today. Notably, the existing fee structure has not increased since 2013, and after twelve years, it makes sense to revisit the fee structure to ensure it keeps pace with inflation and is fair. In this regard, we support the principle behind LD 358 to ensure sufficient fees, but we defer to the Registers of Deeds and other stakeholders with regard to how those fees are best structured.
MCCA also notes that fees paid to the Registry of Deeds help support the important functions of county government, including maintenance of county jails, critical law enforcement services provided by county sheriffs, and needed emergency management services. If the fees paid to the Registries of Deeds do not keep pace with inflation, the contributions made to county government will decline as a percentage of county revenues and the shortfall will need to be made up through local property taxes. In short, if the fees paid to Registries of Deeds do not increase, local property taxpayers will end up paying more in taxes.
As a final note, in supporting LD 358, we recognize that increased fees may burden specific classes of users, including municipal government. If the fees paid by municipalities go up, the costs will ultimately fall to the local property taxpayer. With this in mind, MCCA would support further modifications to the bill to ease burdens on local municipalities.

Testimony of MCCA re LD 358 February 24, 2025 Page 2
Conclusion. We appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony in support of LD 358. Thank you, and if you have questions or need additional information, please do not hesitate to let us know.
Respectfully submitted,

Stephen Gorden Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

Jean-Marie Caterina Co-Chair, Legislative Policy Committee, MCCA

NeauSites Statement on L.D. 358 - An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds
Good morning, my name is John Veroneau, and I represent NeauSites, a Maine-based company with a principle address at 100 Silver St, Portland, ME 04101. NeauSites is a real estate information system dedicated to improving access to real estate data.
I am speaking neither for, nor against, L.D. 358. I want to raise concerns about fair access to public records.
I've been informed by the Cumberland County Registry of Deeds that First American, a title insurance company, is the only entity with a wholesale data contract for these records. Through its subsidiary, Data Tree, it resells these data--data that I have been unable to access under the same terms. I have twice asked the registry of deeds for a similar data contract and twice been refused.
This past Friday, I asked the Cumberland County Registry of Deeds for 1,000 consecutive images and was told they would need to physically print them at a cost of about $1 per page, with no option for electronic delivery.
That same day, I requested 1,000 addresses from First American and was informed that I could upload a list of 10,000 addresses and receive a perfectly appended list of all documents associated at a cost of $50 per address.
Allow me to be clear: I do not oppose private companies packaging and reselling public data if they provide a more efficient means of accessing it. In fact, efficient and secure data retrieval is central to my own business model.
But, if one corporation has exclusive access under terms unavailable to others, the state is granting a monopoly on public records--which is neither fair nor in the public interest.
The best approach is one where manual downloads remain free or low-cost for individuals, while automated access is priced fairly and transparently for companies seeking to use this data.
Maine could generate significant revenue without restricting public access.
I respectfully ask the committee:
1. What exactly does this contract include? 2. What is the pricing structure of this contract? 3. Are other companies allowed to enter into similar agreements and if so, why does only
one entity currently have this level of access? 4. How is this data delivered, and at what frequency?
Finally, I urge the committee to ensure:
1. A fair and efficient system for accessing public records.

2. A clear plan for reinvesting fees into improving storage and access. Thank you for your time and consideration.
John R. Veroneau Founder - NEAUSITES USA LLC john@neausites.com

Greetings Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and honorable members of the Committee. My name is Josh Steirman and I am the Director of Government Relations for the Maine Bankers Association. We are the trade association representing 34 retail banks operating across the State of Maine, with over 9,000 employees in virtually every community state-wide. Last year, our banks provided over $2.5 billion in residential real estate loans, and over $3.2 billion in small business loans. Banks are deeply embedded in their communities: last year, bankers volunteered over 145,000 hours, and donated over $18 million to charitable causes. Maine bankers are your neighbors, working to provide a safe place for deposits, modern technology solutions, fraud protection, a home mortgage, or a small business loan.
The Maine Bankers Association is testifying today in regards to L.D. 358, An Act to Increase Feed Paid to Registers of Deeds. We respectfully oppose the bill.
We are concerned that this is effectively a tax increase on real estate transactions. The additional costs will be likely be borne by regular people, and negatively impact their ability to buy a home and build financial stability. This bill is at odds with the necessary efforts already underway to improve our state's business climate and increase access to affordable housing. Housing costs are widely understood to be an impediment to growing Maine's workforce, but unfortunately this bill would exacerbate the problem and significantly increase costs associate with buying a home.
Although we recognize the budget pressures facing registrars and their need for additional revenue, the bill in front of us today proposes a substantial fee increase. Some of the fee increases contemplated today are a tenfold increase - this scale is concerning. Particularly in light of inflation and rising cost of consumer goods across the economy, we are concerned about such a significant new cost for Maine people.

Good Afternoon, Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and distinguished members of the Committee on State & Local Government,
My name is Krista Simonis and I am the Director of Governmental Affairs at the Maine Credit Union League. Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing
Committee on State and Local Government: I am Senator Rick Bennett of Oxford, and I have the honor of serving 14 communities in Western Maine in the State Senate. I am pleased to cosponsor both LD 358, "An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds."

Last year, at the invitation of the Oxford County Register of Deeds, I met with the association of Registers across the state. They requested I sponsor this bill to increase the fees paid to the office. As you probably know, the Register of Deeds is responsible for recording and maintaining public records related to real estate transactions. In Maine, each
county has at least one registry of deeds office. My constituent and the association made this
request because their offices around the state are incurring rising costs for their work and the current fee structure isn't covering those costs nor is it even beginning to cover the work
mandated that they do under statute.

The current fee structure, updated in 2011, is very confusing. It requires payment of $19.00
for the first page of a document and $2.00 for each additional page. On top of that, it requires $1.00 for each name on the document over 4 names and a marginal reference fee of
$13.00 for each reference over 1 reference. There are also additional fees if there is not enough of a margin at the top for recording information. So, instead of a complicated structure, they proposed transitioning to a flat $45 fee for all documents, regardless of the
number of pages.

While evaluating the revenues, the Register of Deeds Association reviewed data from other
New England states and learned that Maine's current fees are significantly lower than our neighbors' . And the increase proposed would still keep us in the lower end compared to the rest of New England.

The original legislative intent of this statute was for the public to have easier access to their
own documents. However, the current structure is so complicated that it often results in
rejection of the submission due to incorrect payment. This causes frustration, delay, additional mailing costs, and increased work for the register of deeds offices. The Maine Registry of Deeds Association is confident that a flat fee structure would eliminate the majority of rejections that are due to incorrect payment amounts.

On top of the recording fees, the Register of Deeds charge a preservation fee. This $3
preservation fee was established in 1997 and has never been increased despite the costs of preservation increasing significantly. This bill proposes to raise that preservation fee from $3 to $5. Even with this additional increase, Maine's fees will be lower than Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Vermont.

Senator Joseph Baldacci, Chair Representative Suzanne Salisbury, Chair Committee on State and Local Government C/O Legislative Information Office 100 State House Station Augusta, ME 04333
Re: Testimony of First American Title Insurance Company on LD 358 - An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds
Chairs Baldacci and Salisbury, and Distinguished Members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government:
First American Title Insurance Company1 (First American) is writing to express concerns about LD 358 - An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds, and to discuss how this legislation will have a negative impact upon access to real property ownership and the ability to do business in Maine. First American is an underwriter of title insurance policies in Maine and works with almost 200 title insurance agents in Maine. These title insurance agents are largely composed of small business owners, including title companies and law firms, that provide settlement services for real estate transactions in Maine.
Increasing access to affordable housing is a priority for the State of Maine and the real estate economy is important to Maine's financial well-being. First American is concerned that LD 358 will have a negative impact upon access to real property ownership, the ability to do business in Maine, and the overall real estate economy for the following reasons:
1. Proposed increase in bulk download fees and prohibition on resale of images will make it more difficult to do business in Maine and have unintended consequences on the general real estate economy. Unlike title companies, closing attorneys, or abstract companies that obtain limited recorded document images for individual real estate transactions, data companies obtain all recorded document images from various county recorders throughout the United States. These data companies make images searchable and available to businesses on a centralized platform for various business purposes. For example, First American Data Tree (Data Tree) makes images available via its username and password protected website to customers as follows:
a. To attorneys conducting research on real property related to estate planning and probate matters.
b. To appraisers preparing appraisals on properties. c. To real estate agents to assist with market research.
1 First American Title Insurance Company is a subsidiary of First American Financial Corporation (NYSE:FAF), one of the nation's largest title insurance companies and providers of real estate settlement services.
707 Sable Oaks Drive, Suite 370, South Portland, ME 04106 T E L 207-774-6884 � F A X 7 1 4 -913-6782

d. To lenders and servicers in connection with loan servicing, fraud detection, and portfolio monitoring.
e. For fraud alert services to alert homeowners of new recordings against their properties.

Businesses that reside outside of the county or the state, or businesses that lack experience obtaining document images from the county recorder directly, rely on companies like Data Tree to provide document images in a centralized, searchable platform. A prohibition on the resale of images or a dramatic fee increase to obtain images would limit data companies' ability to provide these valuable services to businesses as it relates to properties in Maine. Many of the functions above directly benefit Maine residents and further, if data companies are unable to provide these services via centralized platforms, it may result in increased costs being passed on to Maine residents.

LD 358 proposes to increase the fee per image for bulk downloads from $.05 per image to $.50 per image, a tenfold increase in the cost. The table below reflects how Data Trace alone would be financially impacted by the changes proposed by LD 358 based on their recent download requests in just two Maine counties.

County Name Cumberland Waldo

Images in 2024 229,165 35,531

Cost Today $11,458 $1,777

Cost under LD 358 $114,083 $17, 266

In short, the tenfold increase in bulk image fees and the prohibition on resale of images as proposed by LD 358 will make it impossible for Data Tree and similar businesses to continue doing business in Maine.

2. Proposed increase in copy fees will increase the cost of doing business in Maine, unfairly impact small businesses, and limit access to public records. LD 358 proposed to reduce the number of free images (i.e. "copies") that may be downloaded from a county registry of deeds website from 500 to 100 per calendar year, a significant decrease. Currently, each person in Maine may download 500 free images from each of Maine's 17 registries of deeds. Title companies, title examiners and attorneys in Maine regularly access the public records posted on the websites of the registers of deeds for the purpose of examining title to real estate. A title examination or title search is an essential element of every real estate transaction and is performed for the purchase of real estate, the refinance of a mortgage or to obtain a home equity line of credit. A title search may also be performed for other purposes as well, such as part of estate planning process. Here is an example of how LD 358 could financially impact a small business in Maine which actively provides settlement services to Maine consumers. Title Company A employs 25 employees in Maine, 3 of whom regularly perform title searches in Maine's 17 registries of deeds. Title Company A performs an average of 3000 title searches each year and downloads on average 25 images from the registry website as a part of a single title search. Reducing the number of free images from 500 to 100 will cost Title Company A an additional $10,200 in copy fees per year. For residential transactions, copy fees associated with a title search are typically absorbed by title companies and law firms as part of flat fee pricing. These additional costs could be passed on to the consumer. In either situation, the overall cost of the real estate transaction will be increased, either to the detriment of the Maine consumer or to the detriment of Maine's small businesses.

3. Proposed change to recording fees will increase costs for consumers and create additional financial barriers to home ownership. LD 358 proposes to change the fee for recording a document in the registry of deed from $19 for the first page, with $2 for each additional page, and a preservation surcharge of $3 to a flat fee of $45 with a preservation fee of $5 ($50 total). Currently, the average cost for recording a deed is $24 and the average cost of recording a mortgage is $60. Under LD 358, the recording fees for a real estate purchase involving a deed and mortgage, will be increased from an average of $84 to $100. This $16 increase may seem minimal, but this comparison does not tell the whole story. Many residential real estate transactions include the recording of other instruments, such as affidavits, trustee certifications, powers of attorney, partial releases of mortgage, and assignments of mortgage. Currently, the average cost for recording these types of instruments are as follows: Affidavit - $22, Trustee Certification - $22, Power of Attorney - $30, Partial Release of Mortgage - $22, Assignment of Mortgage -$26. LD 358 proposes to increase the recording fee for each of these types of instruments to $50. These additional costs will be borne by the sellers and buyers to the real estate transaction and increase the overall cost of a real estate closing.
First American believes that a well-functioning registry of deeds is crucial to maintaining accurate and accessible public records and we support the concept of predictability in recording fees. However, we are concerned that the increase in the fee structure and the limitation on the use of public records proposed by LD 358 must be balanced against the negative impact on Maine's consumers, Maine's small business owners, and the real estate economy. We, therefore, respectfully encourage this Committee to vote "Ought Not to Pass" on LD 358.
Thank you for your time and consideration and for the opportunity to provide feedback on LD 358.
Sincerely,
By: ________________________________ Robin D. Watts, Maine State Counsel

My name is Samantha Tibbetts. I am a resident of Gardiner and a real estate and title attorney at Central Maine Title Company and Cumberland Title Services (hereinafter "Central Maine Title") in Augusta. I am testifying in opposition to Section 6 of LD 358.
Central Maine Title is a small title company in Maine. We offer title and closing services to lenders and buyers across the state, and to do so we conduct title searches in the registry of deeds to prepare title commitments and abstracts of title to our clients. Many small businesses, like ours, utilize the 500 free copies that the registry provides for documents that are essential to the operation of our business. Contrary to what the registry believes, we do not pass on any document fees paid to the registry to conduct our title examination and final report. The title industry has to maintain competitive pricing for title examinations and closings in order to preserve business on a large scale. If the registry scales back from 500 free copies to 100 free copies per year, our company and other title companies in the industry will be greatly affected, and prices will undoubtedly increase for our clients. The number of free copies that the registry chose to scale back to seems arbitrary. With a significant increase in the fees paid to the registry of deeds, if the bill passes, the registry should be able to maintain the current rate of 500 free copies. For the reasons listed above, I would like to encourage the Committee to consider revising the bill to maintain 500 free copies that the registry provides for currently.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony to the Committee.
Best,

LD: 358 An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds
Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on State and Local Government:
My name is Susan Bulay, I am the Register of Deeds for Penobscot County, and am speaking today on
behalf of the Maine Registers of Deeds Association in favor of LD 358 An Act to Increase Fees Paid to
Registers of Deeds.
The Registry of Deeds for each county, and there are two registries in Aroostook County, is the office of
public notice for all documents relating to real property in our respective counties. We record deeds, mortgages, tax liens, discharges and many other documents submitted to us. We index the document so it can be found, image and microfihn it for posterity. We do all of this for a one time fee which we are
seeking to increase through this legislation. Although the title of the bill is An Act to Increase Fees Paid to Registers of Deeds, please note that this money does not go to us personally but to the county general fund through our department. The name could be slightly misleading.
The current fee structure established in 2011 is: $19.00 for the first page and $2.00 for each additional page per document, plus $1.00 for each name on the document over 4 names, plus a marginal reference fee of $13.00 for each reference over l reference and additional fees if there is not a sufficient top margin for
recording information. We propose to do away with this confusing fee structure and go to a flat fee of
$45.00 per document, plus the restoration surcharge which I will mention later.
The documents for a typical property purchase would include a deed, 2-3 pages with a current fee of $21-
$23, and a mortgage. The mortgage could be 18 pages, with a VA rider, or a manufactured home rider plus
a description for a total of 20 to 24 pages and a current fee of $57-$65. Recording fees for the purchase package, therefore, would be $78-$88. With a flat fee of $45 per document, two documents would be a
new recording fee of $90, plus surcharge. Not so very much different.
We get so many of our submissions from across the country these days, that we feel a flat fee will greatly
reduce the returns of unrecordable documents for lack of proper funds. And it will benefit any homebuyer
at closing because their closing costs will be able to be estimated earlier in the process. If the attomey needs to add pages to a document, there will be no adjustment in fees.
Likewise, we wish to increase the cost of recording plans from $21.00 to $45.00, plus the restoration
surcharge. While original documents are returned once the recording process has been done, plans remain
in our office forever. We do not return them, but must provide permanent storage.
We propose to increase the cost of producing a copy of a plan from $5.00 to $10.00. We have been getting
some push from the surveying community to record and reproduce plans in color. Color wide-format plan scanners and printers cost more than black and white and the size of a color plan file is much larger than a
black and white one. New machines and more storage costs more money.
In 2013, as our websites were gaining in popularity, the legislature felt that we should give our constituents free access to their personal documents so the 500 free copies were introduced. The intent at that time Was
Visit our website: https://PenobscotDeeds.com

that this would benefit the individual homeowner who wanted a copy of their deed and mortgage. There was never any intent that a title company would get free copies to do their business. Most title companies
pay for their copies and then pass on the cost to the consumer, but some have not been as honest. We have
found that some title companies have worked around the legislative intent and have found ways to get all free copies. Therefore we are proposing that bulk image prices be changed from 5 cents per image to 50 cents per image and that companies be prohibited from selling these images for their monetary gain. Bulk sales do not include our indexes, which are proprietary and not for sale. And that the number of fi'ee copies available to an individual be reduced fi'om 500 to 100 free copies per year. After the free copies have been used up the cost is 50 cents per page. The individual who wants a copy of their deed, usually two pages, and a copy of their mortgage, usually 20 pages, would not be impacted by this change to better align the
statute with the original legislative intent. In anticipation of an amendment by Sen. Bennett, let me add that
we have no intention of creating a hardship for the town assessors. We feel that by setting our computer
systems to allow the towns unlimited free copies from the web site, they can still do their job as they currently are and we can limit the title companies from taking advantage of the county. In addition to the recording fee, we also collect a recording surcharge of $3.00 per document to pay for ongoing restoration of our documents and plans, including digitizing all documents so that the public may access them easier. This surcharge was enacted in 1997 and has never been increased, however, in the
meantime, the costs of preservation have increased significantly. We propose to increase this to $5.00 per
document. Currently the state and our municipalities are exempt from this surcharge and we propose to
'
continue that exemption.
In addition, the registers must report to this committee every year how much surcharge money we raised
and how much we expended. We have complied with this requirement faithfully, but I know of no other
entity that must do this type of reporting and we would like to suspend the surcharge reporting unless this
committee specifically requests us to present it.
Please bear in mind that our fees are one time fees collected only when a document is recorded. This is not like your municipal property taxes or automobile registration which are collected every year. When you record a document you pay for the recording process and for perpetual care. The records in York County go back to 1638; in Penobscot County we go back to 1814. Every registry has every document ever recorded in that office. For a one time fee. Please also remember that revenue in excess of expenses is
allocated to the general fund of the county to lower the tax obligations for the towns.
We urge you to vote ought to pass on LD 358 and, as always, we are happy to answer any question at any
time.
